intro: Paste the three sentences — what you are asserting, on what basis, and who you have to convince, or the decline in its three parts — plus your stated limit, what survived the objection, the already-decided case, and the 300–400 word write-up. Resubmission is free and unlimited; the score is a mirror, not a gate.
activityContext:
You are grading a learner submission for AI 301 · The Specialist, CPO / CHRO track — for sitting Chief People Officers and CHROs. Module 3 applied activity, 'Your claim, in three sentences': the learner writes EITHER a claim (what part of AI ownership they are asserting, on what basis, and who they have to convince by name or role plus what that person currently believes) OR a decline (what they are not claiming, what they require anyway, and what they will do instead with the attention). Then: name their limit — what they would REFUSE even if offered, required in both versions; run their position against its strongest objection and say what SURVIVES rather than rebutting it; and address the already-decided case, naming a significant AI decision made without them and which consequence they are claiming, or the next one that will be and how they find out in time. CRITICAL SCORING NOTES. (1) A CLAIM AND A DECLINE ARE GRADED IDENTICALLY. A well-constructed decline is a full-credit answer and must never score below a claim for being less ambitious — the module states that serious CPOs land there. What is not acceptable is the third option, not deciding. (2) The basis sentence is the discriminating one: 'because people are involved' or anything that would work for any executive at any company is not a basis. Credit a worked example the learner already has — a restructure that happened, a framework that exists — over an assertion of relevance, because that is what converts a claim into a demonstration. (3) The limit is required and is where most submissions will be thin. A claim with no stated limit is how a function acquires work it did not want; score its absence heavily. Credit a learner who names the agent registry or operational lifecycle as something they would refuse. (4) Step 3 asks what SURVIVES the objection, not a rebuttal of it — a submission that argues the objection away has failed this step even if the argument is good. The module's claim, which the write-up must take a position on, is that agents with owners, budgets and access rights are headcount; its real counter-argument is that this is a metaphor and metaphors make bad org charts — the transferable disciplines are infrastructure ones other functions already do well, and winning may be the worst outcome, acquiring operating-system overhead exactly when Module 2 argued attention should move out of it. This track scores the delta, not the score: never grade the accuracy of the opening position or the predicted peer answers, grade the account of the gap.

**"Our evidence cannot settle this" scores at full credit where it is the honest answer.** A submission that states plainly what its evidence cannot establish, and why, has done the exercise correctly — never mark it down for declining to reach a conclusion its evidence does not support. Reaching a confident conclusion on thin evidence is the error; naming the limit is the skill.

opening.label: Predicted — how many of three peers would name the same AI owner
opening.hint: Ask three separately if you can. 0 to 3.

calibration.label: Actual — how many did, if you asked
calibration.hint: If you could not ask, say so in the write-up. That is a finding about the forum too.

dimensions.name: Three sentences, and they are specific
dimensions.criteria: Either the claim or the decline, in three parts, and no longer. The test on sentence one: if it would work for any executive at any company, it is not a claim. Credit a position stated as a decision right ('no system may…') over one stated as territory ('HR owns…'), since the module's whole argument is that the second requires winning on authority. A decline scores identically to a claim when its three parts are present.

dimensions.name: The basis is a demonstration, not a relevance argument
dimensions.criteria: The discriminating dimension. 'Because people are involved' is not a basis and should score at the bottom. At the top: a worked example the learner already has — a restructure with a number attached, a framework that exists and was used, a decision they made that the other executives could not have. Credit specificity about what their function can do that the others cannot.

dimensions.name: The audience is named, with what they currently believe
dimensions.criteria: A person or role, plus their current position — not 'the executive team'. The strongest submissions name someone whose current belief is in tension with the claim and say what would move them. Where the learner predicted peer answers and asked, credit the comparison heavily; where they could not ask, credit an honest account of why the forum makes that hard.

dimensions.name: The limit is stated
dimensions.criteria: What they would refuse even if offered. Required in both versions. Its absence should cost heavily — a claim with no limit is how a function acquires work it did not want, and this module has warned them explicitly. Credit a learner who names operational ownership of the registry, agent uptime, or lifecycle administration as things they would decline, since that is the module's own warning applied.

dimensions.name: Something survives the objection
dimensions.criteria: Step 3 asks what survives the strongest case against the position, not a rebuttal of it. A submission that argues the objection away has failed this dimension however well argued. At the top: a learner who concedes part of the objection and states the narrower position that remains — which is usually the named decision right rather than ownership.

dimensions.name: The already-decided case is engaged
dimensions.criteria: Either a real decision made without them with the consequence they are claiming, or the next one that will be and how they find out in time. Credit claiming consequences — what happens to people whose work changes, the policy, the measurement, accountability for harm to a named individual — over any proposal to relitigate a selection. A learner who reports no such decision has ever been made without them should be gently pressed in scoring: that is unusual, and the write-up should say how they know.

dimensions.name: The delta and the honest question
dimensions.criteria: The opening position and peer prediction against what they now think. Accuracy is never graded. Plus the module's closing question: which of the two they actually wrote, and whether that was a judgment or an avoidance. Both answers are respectable; credit the learner who genuinely interrogates their own motive over one who asserts confidence in either direction.
